title: Madd wājib muttaṣil
objectives: Student can identify a madd letter followed by a hamzah inside the same word, on sight, from the maddah ٓ plus the position of the hamzah.
Student can hold four counts cleanly and land the hamzah crisply at the end of it, at full volume.
Student can say why this madd is wājib — obligatory for every reciter, with no two-count option anywhere.
Student can state the consistency rule: muttaṣil is held at one length for the whole session, and is never shorter than munfaṣil.

slides.heading: Read this. You already can.
body: إِذَا جَآءَ نَصْرُ ٱللَّهِ وَٱلْفَتْحُ — the opening of an-Naṣr, which you hold by heart.
You will almost certainly read جَآءَ at two counts. Then, because the hamzah is hard work after a long vowel, you will either swallow the hamzah or smear the whole word into jaa.
I read it back to you twice: once your way, once at four counts with a clean hamzah landing on the end.
There is a wiggle over that alif. You read straight past it. That mark is the single most reliable instruction in the whole muṣḥaf, and from today you never read past one again.
You have been reading this word short since Unit 2 and nothing has ever contradicted you. That is why the correction lands so hard.

audio.cue: 110:1 — maddah over the alif, hamzah immediately after it, same word. Four counts, then a hamzah you can hear as a separate event.

slides.translation: When the help of Allah has come, and the victory.

audio.cue: جَآءَ at four counts. Hold — hold — hold — hold — close. The hamzah arrives at full volume, not as an afterthought.

slides.heading: What you already have
body: The three madd letters and a clean two counts, from 3-28.
The maddah ٓ means longer than two. Today you get your first actual number for it.
The five-row map from last lesson. Point at the second row: hamzah, same word.
Hamzah as a letter with its own makhraj, from Phase 1 — including that it is a stop, an articulated closure, and not a vowel.

slides.heading: Madd wājib muttaṣil — four counts, obligatory
slides.condition: A madd letter followed by a hamzah, in the same word.
slides.mnemonic: The hamzah is the cause; the madd is the room the tongue needs to reach it.
body: Write جَآءَ large. Put a finger over the hamzah. What is left is a plain two-count madd. Now uncover the hamzah.
The hamzah is heavy, it is hard to say, and the tongue needs room to get to it. The madd is the room.
That is not a mnemonic — it is close to the reason the classical sources give. The hamzah is the deepest and most effortful letter, and the extra length is the approach to it.
Because cause and madd live inside one word, nothing can ever separate them. That is why the ruling is wājib rather than jāʾiz.
Four counts. There is no reading of the Qurʾān in which جَآءَ is two.

slides.heading: Why wājib — and the contrast that is coming
body: Wājib means obligatory, and here it is meant literally: every qāriʾ in every ṭarīq lengthens this beyond two counts.
Next lesson's rule, munfaṣil, has the hamzah in the NEXT word. Stop on the first word and the cause is gone.
Muttaṣil: same word · never separable · wājib · shortest correct length 4.
Munfaṣil: next word · separable by a stop · jāʾiz · 2 is correct in another ṭarīq.
Give her the argument, not the fact. The ruling follows from the spelling, which means she can derive it instead of memorising it.

slides.heading: The length: four or five, and then hold it
body: Four or five ḥarakāt, via ṭarīq ash-Shāṭibiyyah — four in ḥadr and tadwīr, five in slow tartīl.
This course pins 4–5, matching the Ḥuṣarī recitation used throughout. Choose one — four while learning, because it is audible without being ponderous — and then hold it.
Consistency rule one: one length for the whole session. Four in one āyah and five in the next is the actual error. Neither number is.
Consistency rule two: muttaṣil is never shorter than munfaṣil. You do not know why yet. You get the rule today and the reason at 3-30.
Say both of them back to me before we go on.

slides.heading: Landing the hamzah
body: Half of this lesson is length. The other half is the letter at the end of it, and the second half is what you will actually get wrong in three weeks' time.
After four counts of open vowel the throat is relaxed and the hamzah wants to disappear.
Drill the shape explicitly: hold — hold — hold — hold — close.
The hamzah is a clean glottal closure and release. It arrives at full volume, not as an afterthought.
Say جَآءَ with an exaggerated, almost percussive hamzah four or five times, then dial it back to normal. Overshooting first is the fastest route to normal.

slides.translation: Those who make show of their deeds.

audio.cue: يُرَآءُونَ — a muttaṣil inside al-Māʿūn, which you are memorising right now. Four counts, every single time you recite this surah from today onward.

slides.translation: Their accustomed security in the caravan of winter and summer.

audio.cue: ٱلشِّتَآءِ — a muttaṣil in Quraysh, which reaches your hifz in three lessons. Preview it now so the four counts are already there when you memorise it.

slides.heading: Two rules you meet inside your own hifz
body: يُرَآءُونَ is in al-Māʿūn, which you are memorising this week. ٱلشِّتَآءِ is in Quraysh, which you reach in two lessons.
Spend your time on those two, not on the textbook examples.
A rule she meets inside material she is memorising gets rehearsed twenty times a day without any extra homework. A rule she meets only in a textbook gets rehearsed once.
That is why this lesson previews Quraysh rather than waiting for it.

slides.heading: Spotting it on the page — two questions, in order
body: One: is there a ٓ over a madd letter? If no, it is two counts. Move on and do not think about it.
Two: where is the hamzah that caused it? Same word → muttaṣil, four. Next word → munfaṣil, which is next lesson.
That is the entire visual procedure and it will serve you for both rules.
Practise it as a silent scan before you read — eyes only, no sound. Doing it mid-recitation is too late, and the hesitation costs you a fluency mark even when the answer is right.
Reference examples from outside your memorised surahs, to read from the page: ٱلسَّمَآءِ (2:19), سُوٓءًا (4:110) with a wāw madd rather than an alif, ٱلْأَسْمَآءَ (2:31), and لِلْمَلَٰٓئِكَةِ (2:30).

slides.heading: The stop that buys a sixth count
body: Say this once, clearly, and do not drill it hard today.

If you stop on the word-final hamzah itself — as in ٱلشِّتَآءِ, or in ٱلسَّمَآءِ (2:19) — the sukūn of stopping stacks onto the hamzah and six counts becomes permitted. Some name this madd muttaṣil ʿāriḍ.
It is the same mechanism you meet properly at 3-31.
Your practical instruction for now: join → four. Stop on the hamzah → four is still fine, six is also fine.
You do not have to use the six. You do have to not be confused when you hear it.

slides.heading: Where it is not — two traps
body: A hamzah BEFORE the madd letter is irrelevant. وَءَامَنَهُم in 106:4 — the hamzah comes first, and the alif after it is a different rule, madd badal, at two counts.
The question you are answering is always: does the hamzah come before or after the madd letter?

The second trap is the opposite. A dagger alif still counts. لِلْمَلَٰٓئِكَةِ (2:30) is muttaṣil: the alif is superscript, the maddah sits on top of it, and the hamzah follows it inside the same word.
You will miss that one. Everyone does, because the eye reads a superscript stroke as a vowel mark rather than as a letter — which is exactly the leak 3-28 was about.
Say اللهم آمين at the end of al-Fātiḥah and notice that ءَامِين is not a muttaṣil. Be ready to tell me why.

slides.heading: Four, or two? The hamzah decides by where it stands

pairs.note: Alif madd, then a hamzah, same word. Four counts. The hamzah comes AFTER the madd letter, so it is the cause.
Hamzah first, then the alif. The hamzah cannot cause a madd it precedes. Two counts — madd badal, a ṭabīʿī-length relative.
Sun-letter shadda at the front, then madd before a hamzah. Four counts joined; six is also open to you if you stop on the hamzah.
A dagger alif with no maddah over it and no hamzah after it. Plain two. A superscript alif is not automatically anything.

slides.heading: Cover the hamzah
slides.instructions: I show you a muttaṣil word with the hamzah covered by my thumb. Read what you see: two counts. I lift my thumb. Read it again: four counts and a clean hamzah. Alternate until the four arrives without you deciding on it.

audio.cue: Covered: جَا, two counts. Uncovered: four counts and shut the door on the end of it.
107:6 — covered, a plain two-count alif. Uncovered, four counts and then a hamzah, and only then the wāw madd.
106:2 — covered, two. Uncovered, four. The maddah told you before the thumb moved.

slides.heading: The ladder
slides.instructions: Take جَآءَ and read it four times: at two, at four, at five, at six. Then tell me which one is wrong, and why.

audio.cue: At TWO — this is the wrong one. It is the only length that is never permitted anywhere, in any ṭarīq.
At FOUR — correct, and the length this course asks you to hold.
At FIVE — also correct, the slow-tartīl length. Correct, but not if you gave four in the āyah before.
At SIX — only available if you STOP on the hamzah. Here you are joining onward, so six is not yours.

slides.heading: The percussive hamzah
slides.instructions: Say each one with the hamzah far too hard, five times. Then say it normally. Listen for whether the hamzah is still fully there once you stop pushing.

audio.cue: Four flat counts, then shut the throat. I want to hear the door close.
The hardest of the three: the hamzah is in the middle of the word, so there is nothing after it to hide behind.
Four counts, hamzah at full volume, and then the kasrah on it. Do not let the madd rise in pitch as it approaches.

mistakes.wrong: Two counts on جَآءَ, ٱلشِّتَآءِ, يُرَآءُونَ.
mistakes.why: She has read these words for years without the rule, and the maddah has never meant anything to her before. Habit, not ignorance.
mistakes.fix: Point at the wiggle. That mark has been there the whole time. It means four.

mistakes.wrong: The hamzah is swallowed — jaa, ash-shitaa.
mistakes.why: The throat relaxes across a long vowel and cannot re-close in time. It is a physical timing failure, not carelessness.
mistakes.fix: Hold the aaa, and then shut it. I want to hear the door close.

mistakes.wrong: The madd swells or rises in pitch before the hamzah lands.
mistakes.why: She is bracing for the hamzah and the effort leaks backwards into the vowel.
mistakes.fix: Flat. All four counts at the same pitch, then the hamzah. Don't announce it.

mistakes.wrong: Four counts in one āyah, five in the next.
mistakes.why: She is producing each madd from scratch rather than from a held tempo. This is the most common error of the whole unit and it will persist.
mistakes.fix: Both are correct. Both in one page is not. Pick four, and give me four every time today.

mistakes.wrong: Lengthening وَءَامَنَهُم, or any word where the hamzah comes first.
mistakes.why: Over-generalisation from today — she has learned 'hamzah plus madd means long' without the order.
mistakes.fix: Which came first, the hamzah or the alif? Hamzah first is not this rule.

mistakes.wrong: Missing the muttaṣil on a dagger alif, as in لِلْمَلَٰٓئِكَةِ.
mistakes.why: The superscript stroke does not read to the eye as a letter, so the maddah on top of it does not read as attached to anything.
mistakes.fix: That stroke is an alif. The wiggle is sitting on it. Where is the hamzah? Same word. Four.

slides.heading: Four counts, and where they come from

audio.cue: FOUR — alif madd, hamzah, same word. The reference case.
FOUR — in al-Māʿūn, which you are memorising. Four every time from today.
FOUR joined, SIX permitted if you stop on the hamzah. Never two.
TWO — the hamzah is in front of the madd letter, not behind it. Different rule entirely.
TWO — a dagger alif with no maddah and no hamzah. Plain ṭabīʿī.

slides.heading: Homework
tasks: Hifz: al-Māʿūn 107:1–2 as the new Sabaq, 20–40 repetitions daily. Sabqi is al-Kawthar, every single session. Manzil rotation first. Ten extra repetitions after any caught error, logged on its own line.

The silent scan on one fresh page: mark every ٓ, and label each one M if the hamzah is in the same word and N if it is in the next. Bring the marked page. You are not asked to read it correctly — you are asked to SEE it correctly.
Read Sūrat al-Māʿūn from the page, not from memory, once a day, and give يُرَآءُونَ four counts every time, even though you have not formally reached it in your memorisation.
Write out five muttaṣil words you find anywhere in the last juzʾ, with the sūrah and āyah number for each. If you cannot find five, bring three and we will look together.
Say اللهم آمين at the end of al-Fātiḥah and notice that ءَامِين is not a muttaṣil. Be ready to tell me why.

drills.title: Cover the hamzah
drills.instructions: Thumb over the hamzah: two counts. Thumb lifted: four counts and a clean close. Ten alternations.

audio.cue: Covered two, uncovered four.
Covered two, uncovered four, then the wāw madd after the hamzah.
Covered two, uncovered four.

drills.title: The consistency check
drills.instructions: Read a passage containing three or more muttaṣil. Nothing is being timed except whether all three are the same length as each other. One inconsistency and you start the passage again.

audio.cue: Whatever number you picked. Same number here.
Same number again. Not longer because it is newer to you.
Same number a third time. Three matched lengths is the whole exercise.

drills.title: The badal trap
drills.instructions: Read each pair back to back and say which is four and which is two before you sound either one. The question is always: does the hamzah come before or after the madd letter?

audio.cue: FOUR — hamzah after.
TWO — hamzah before.
FOUR — hamzah after.
TWO — no hamzah at all, and no maddah either.

dailyChecklist: Al-Māʿūn 107:1–2 to 20–40 repetitions, with al-Kawthar as Sabqi and the Manzil rotation first
Sūrat al-Māʿūn read from the page once, with يُرَآءُونَ at four counts every time
Cover-the-hamzah on the three reference words, ten alternations
One page silently scanned: every ٓ marked, each one labelled M or N
The badal pairs called out before reading — four or two, decided by where the hamzah stands

script: Open on 110:1, which she can already read. She will give جَآءَ two counts and either swallow or smear the hamzah. Read it back to her twice — her way, then yours — before saying anything analytical.
The corrective value here is unusually high because nothing has ever contradicted her on this word. Say that out loud: the mark has been on the page the whole time.

Cover the hamzah with your thumb and let her see the word become a plain two-count madd. The hamzah as cause, and the madd as the room the tongue needs to reach it, is close to the classical reasoning and not a teaching fiction — give it as a reason, not a mnemonic.

Make the wājib/jāʾiz contrast do the work of the ruling. Because cause and madd live in one word, nothing can separate them; therefore obligatory. She can derive it, which means she will not need to memorise it.

Give both consistency rules today and be explicit that the second one — muttaṣil is never shorter than munfaṣil — comes without its reason until 3-30. Flagging the deferral is what stops it feeling like a gap in the system.
Spend half the session on landing the hamzah, not on length. Length is what she will get right this week; the hamzah is what she will lose in three weeks.
Overshoot deliberately: a percussive, exaggerated hamzah five times, then normal. Overshooting first is the fastest route to normal and it costs ninety seconds.
Prioritise يُرَآءُونَ and ٱلشِّتَآءِ over the textbook examples. A rule that lives inside the surah she is memorising gets twenty rehearsals a day for free.
Mention the six-count-at-a-stop option once and do not drill it. She needs to not be confused when she hears it; she does not need to produce it until 3-31.

Close on the badal trap, and let her answer the ءَامِين question herself next session rather than telling her. It is the cleanest test of whether she has the ORDER of the rule or only its ingredients.

listenFor.item: Four steady counts, and then a hamzah audible as a separate event at the end of them.
listenFor.commonMistake: Two counts on جَآءَ, ٱلشِّتَآءِ, يُرَآءُونَ.
listenFor.whyItHappens: She has read these words for years without the rule, and the maddah has never meant anything to her. This is habit, not ignorance, and it will not respond to being told the rule again.
listenFor.correctionCue: Point at the wiggle. That mark has been there the whole time. It means four.

listenFor.item: A clean glottal closure and release at the end of the madd, at full volume.
listenFor.makhraj: The hamzah is a full closure of the vocal folds — the deepest point of the throat — released cleanly, not a breathy approximation of one.
listenFor.commonMistake: The hamzah is swallowed: jaa, ash-shitaa.
listenFor.whyItHappens: The throat relaxes across four counts of open vowel and cannot re-close in time. It is a physical timing failure rather than carelessness.
listenFor.correctionCue: Hold the aaa, and then shut it. I want to hear the door close.

listenFor.item: A flat madd — no rise in pitch or volume as the hamzah approaches.
listenFor.commonMistake: The madd swells or climbs just before the hamzah lands.
listenFor.whyItHappens: She is bracing for the effort of the hamzah and the effort leaks backwards into the vowel.
listenFor.correctionCue: Flat. All four counts at the same pitch, then the hamzah. Don't announce it.

listenFor.item: Every muttaṣil in the session at the same length as every other one.
listenFor.commonMistake: Four counts in one āyah, five in the next.
listenFor.whyItHappens: She is producing each madd from scratch rather than from a held tempo. This is the dominant error of the whole unit and it persists past the point where the rules are secure.
listenFor.correctionCue: Both are correct. Both in one page is not. Pick four, and give me four every time today.

listenFor.item: Two counts kept on madd badal — a madd letter that FOLLOWS its hamzah.
listenFor.commonMistake: Lengthening وَءَامَنَهُم, ءَامِين, إِيَّاكَ to four.
listenFor.whyItHappens: Over-generalisation on the day of the lesson: she has taken away 'hamzah plus madd means long' without the order of the two.
listenFor.correctionCue: Which came first, the hamzah or the alif? Hamzah first is not this rule.

teacherNotes.homework: Daily: al-Māʿūn 107:1–2 to 20–40 repetitions with al-Kawthar as Sabqi and the Manzil rotation first, ten extra repetitions logged after any caught error; Sūrat al-Māʿūn read from the page once with يُرَآءُونَ given four counts. Written: one fresh page silently scanned, every maddah marked and labelled M or N, brought to the session — she is being marked on seeing it correctly, not on reading it correctly; and five muttaṣil words found anywhere in the last juzʾ with references. One question to answer next session: why ءَامِين is not a muttaṣil.
